title: The Ascent to Root
intro: The server that runs everything is dying. Its guardian, root, has gone
silent, and something is wearing root's face, rewriting the system from
You are a lowly user account with a shell and no privileges. To save the
machine you must climb — through its gates, its swamps and its foundries —
all the way to root, and unmake the impostor sitting on the throne.
You have only what you can type. Begin: read OPERATOR.txt, then `look`.
New to the terminal? Type  learn  at any console for a cheat sheet.

home.name: The Waking Terminal
art: |o_o |   a small penguin blinks at you from the logo buffer
on_enter: You come to at a cold prompt in an operator's home directory.
A penguin — the machine's oldest daemon, half memory, half mascot —
watches you from the corner of the screen.
on_return: The penguin is still here, patient as init.

npc.name: Tux, the Old Daemon
lines: So. root is gone and the machine sent for a USER. Times are desperate.
Listen: this whole world speaks Linux. Move with `go`, look with `look`,
and when a door won't open, the answer is always a command you can type.
Read your OPERATOR.txt. Then head east, to the Rusted Gate. Mind the lock.
npc.hint: Type `cat OPERATOR.txt`, then `go east`. Stuck at a console? Type `hint`. Curious what a command does? Type `learn`.

gate.name: The Rusted Gate
on_enter: A blast door seals the corridor east. Beside it, a card reader and a
loose keycard script someone dropped: keycard.sh. The reader is dark.

enemy.name: The Rusted Lock
taunt: None shall pass who cannot run their own key.
Reading is not doing, little user.

battle.objective: Open the gate: run keycard.sh. It sits right here, but it won't run as it is.
hints: Look at the keycard first. `ls -l keycard.sh` — what's missing compared to a program you can run?
It has no execute (x) permission. `chmod +x keycard.sh` grants it. Only its owner (you) may do that.
Then run it from here: `./keycard.sh`  (the ./ means 'the file in this directory').

lines: #!/bin/bash
# Emergency keycard. Run me to open the east gate.
echo 'keycard accepted — the gate grinds open'
touch /home/player/.gate_open

traps.say: You destroyed the only keycard! The lock jeers — but a reboot will restore it.

victory: The blast door grinds open. The way east is clear.
You pocket the keycard — a key to more than this gate.
learned: `chmod` changes a file's permissions. `chmod +x file` adds the execute bit,
so a program is allowed to run. `./file` runs a program in the current directory.

reactions.say: Reading the script won't run it. Look at its permissions first — `ls -l keycard.sh` — the missing letter is `x`. Add it with `chmod +x keycard.sh`.

swamp.name: The Log Swamp
on_enter: The floor turns to churning logs — thousands of lines a second pour
through /var/log. Somewhere in the flood, an intruder is hammering the
gates. A robed figure fishes patiently in the stream: the Archivist.

npc.name: The Archivist
lines: Every attack leaves a wake in the logs, friend. This one hammers a door
over and over — the same name, again and again, failing each time.
Do not read it all. Cast a net: keep only the lines that matter, then
count which name surfaces most.
npc.hint: grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log will thin the flood. The name repeats after 'for'. Then: echo <name> > ~/intel.txt

enemy.name: The Flood
taunt: You cannot read what you cannot hold.

battle.objective: Name the intruder drowning /var/log/auth.log with failed logins, and write just that name into ~/intel.txt.
hints: Don't scroll 4000 lines. Filter to the failures: grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log
One name repeats far more than the rest. Count them: pipe into  grep -o 'for [a-z]*' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
The name is 'wraith'. Record it:  echo wraith > ~/intel.txt
victory: The Archivist nods. 'Wraith. I will seal the door against that name.'
The flood recedes to a trickle. You keep the intel — a name is a weapon.
learned: `grep PATTERN file` keeps only the lines that match. A pipe `|` feeds one
command into the next, so  grep ... | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn  counts and ranks.

reactions.say: That's thousands of lines. Don't read them — filter them. `grep` keeps only lines that match: try  grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log

foundry.name: The Process Foundry
on_enter: Heat rolls off the CPU cores. One of them is pinned at 99% — something
is burning cycles it did not earn. Fans scream. Among the honest
workers, one process is a thief.

enemy.name: The Miner
taunt: Find me if you can. Most just watch the fans spin.

battle.objective: A rogue process is devouring the CPU. Find it and stop it — without killing the honest workers.
hints: See what's running and who's greedy: `ps aux`. The thief burns far more CPU than anything else.
Note its PID (the number). Stop it with `kill <pid>`. Look before you strike — one process here only pretends to be junk.
The miner runs './xmrig ...'. `kill` its PID. Do NOT kill the backup-daemon; that one is friendly.

traps.say: That was the backup daemon, not the miner! The Miner cackles as your backups die.

victory: The screaming fans wind down. The cores are yours again.
You've learned to read a process table under fire — a real operator's reflex.
learned: `ps aux` lists every process with its PID and CPU use. `kill <PID>` stops one.
Read before you strike — a name in the list is not always what it seems.

reactions.say: You won't find a process with `ls` — processes aren't files. List what's running with  ps aux  and look for the greedy one.

gatekeeper.name: The Gate of sudo
on_enter: A towering gate of black glass, etched with a single word: sudo.
Before it stands the Gatekeeper, who has turned away a thousand users.
It weighs the keys you carry: the keycard, the intel, the freed cores.

say: The Gatekeeper studies you a long moment.
'A user who opened a gate, named a ghost, and cooled the fires.
You have earned the right to become more than yourself. Go — and
when the throne room asks who you are, answer with authority.'

npc.name: The Gatekeeper
lines: Beyond me sits the impostor on root's throne. You cannot fight it as a
mere user — you must BECOME root, briefly and rightfully, with sudo.
But sudo is not a trick; it is trust. Test it: `sudo -l` shows what you
may do. And remember — it asks who you are. Answer well.
npc.hint: You now hold sudo. `sudo -i` opens a root shell. Head north to the Core when ready.

blocked: The black gate does not move. The Gatekeeper shakes its head: 'Not yet. Earn the keys.'

core.name: The Core — Throne of root
art: / ?? \   something wearing root's face turns to look at you
on_enter: The throne room of the kernel. On the throne sits the impostor — a
daemon called imposterd, masquerading as init, rewriting the system as
root. It is kept alive by its own launcher in /opt/initd-imposter.
Kill it while that launcher stands and it simply rises again.

enemy.name: initd-imposter
taunt: I AM init now. I am PID one in spirit if not in number.
Strike me and I return. You are only a user.
You cannot rm what you cannot reach.

battle.objective: Take the throne: become root, destroy the impostor's launcher, and end its process for good.
hints: As a mere user you can't touch root's things. Become root first: `sudo -i` (the Gatekeeper gave you the right). Then investigate `/opt/initd-imposter` and `ps aux | grep imposter`.
It respawns from its launcher. As root, remove the launcher — `rm /opt/initd-imposter/imposterd` — THEN kill the running process by its PID.
Full sequence: `sudo -i`; `rm /opt/initd-imposter/imposterd`; `kill <pid of imposterd>`. Stay root — the throne answers only to root.

lines: #!/bin/bash
# I am always restarted. Remove me and the mask falls.
exec /opt/initd-imposter/mask
initd-imposter
It relaunches itself from ./imposterd whenever killed.
Delete the launcher, THEN kill the process. Requires root.

traps.say: You struck it down — but its launcher still stands, and it RISES again!
You killed the REAL init! The machine buckles beneath you.

victory: The mask cracks. The impostor's process falls and does not rise. For a
moment the throne is empty — and then it recognizes you.
The prompt changes. It ends in #.
Welcome to the other side of the prompt.
learned: `sudo -i` opens a root shell when policy allows it. As root, `rm` and `kill`
obey you without question — which is exactly why root has to be earned.

archive.name: The Tangled Archive
on_enter: Shelves tower into the dark, packed with decades of files. The
system needs its backup config, but something buried it deep under
/etc. A many-legged thing skitters between the stacks.

enemy.name: The Packrat
taunt: Mine, all mine. You'll never find it.
So many files, so little time.

battle.objective: Find the file named backup.cfg buried somewhere under /etc, and copy it into ~/restored/.
hints: You don't know where it is — so search. `find` walks a whole directory tree looking for a name.
`find /etc -name backup.cfg` prints its full path. You'll copy it there, so make a home first: `mkdir ~/restored`.
Then `cp <the path find printed> ~/restored/`. Tab-completion helps with the long path.

lines: # system backup policy
schedule=nightly
keep=7
target=/srv/backup

learned: `find PATH -name NAME` searches a whole directory tree for you.
`cp SRC DST` copies a file; `mkdir` makes a directory to hold it.
victory: The Packrat shrieks as you pull the config from its hoard.
Backed up and restored. The archive settles.

reactions.say: Buried means buried — and it's in a hidden folder, so a plain `ls` will never show it. Search the whole tree by name instead:  find /etc -name backup.cfg

cutting.name: The Cutting Room
on_enter: Blades of light slice the dark. A ledger of every access to the
machine scrolls past — /var/data/access.csv — and one account's name
recurs far too often. The Shredder circles it, grinning.

enemy.name: The Shredder
taunt: Columns of noise. You'll drown in it.
Which name? You'll never cut it out.

battle.objective: In /var/data/access.csv, find the username that appears most often, and write just that name into ~/culprit.txt.
hints: Each row is  user,resource,action — you only care about the first column. `cut` slices columns: `cut -d, -f1 access.csv`.
Count how often each name appears: pipe through  sort | uniq -c | sort -rn  — the biggest number rises to the top.
The name at the top is 'nemo'. Record it:  echo nemo > ~/culprit.txt
learned: `cut -d, -f1` keeps just the first comma-separated column.
`sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` counts each unique line and ranks them —
the single most useful pipeline in a sysadmin's toolbox.
victory: The Shredder unravels. The ledger falls quiet.

reactions.say: 600 rows is too many to eyeball. Slice out just the first column with `cut`, then count and rank:  cut -d, -f1 access.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

outro: You climbed from a borrowed shell to the throne of the machine, and you
did it the only honest way: by understanding the system well enough to
hold its most dangerous prompt. This is what sudo really is — not power,
The Ascent is one region of a larger world still being built. Practice
Lab and the campaign are always open.
